## Setup and Key Reduction

**Unimodal permutations.** A permutation $\pi$ is *unimodal* if $\pi(1) < \cdots < \pi(k) > \pi(k+1) > \cdots > \pi(n)$ for some $k$. The peak value must be $n$ (the maximum), so each unimodal permutation is determined by the subset $S \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ of elements placed to the left of $n$ (in increasing order), with the rest to the right (in decreasing order). This gives $|U_n| = 2^{n-1}$.

**Reduction.** Since $f \circ \sigma$ ranges over all permutations as $f$ ranges over $S_n$, we have $G_\sigma = \{f : f \circ \sigma \in U_n\}$, so $|G_\sigma| = 2^{n-1}$ for every $\sigma$.

Setting $g = f \circ \sigma$ and $\rho = \sigma^{-1} \circ \tau$, the intersection becomes:
$$|G_\sigma \cap G_\tau| = |\{g \in U_n : g \circ \rho \in U_n\}|$$
which depends only on $\rho$. As $\sigma, \tau$ range over $S_n$, $\rho$ ranges over all of $S_n$.

## Computing $M(n)$

**Upper bound:** $|G_\sigma \cap G_\tau| \leq |G_\sigma| = 2^{n-1}$.

**Achieving the bound:** Take $\rho = \text{id}$ (i.e., $\sigma = \tau$), giving $|G_\sigma \cap G_\tau| = 2^{n-1}$.

Even if $\sigma \neq \tau$ is required, take $\rho = \text{rev}$ (the reversal, $\text{rev}(i) = n+1-i$). If $g = (a_1, \ldots, a_k, n, b_1, \ldots, b_m)$ is unimodal with $a_1 < \cdots < a_k < n > b_1 > \cdots > b_m$, then:
$$g \circ \text{rev} = (b_m, \ldots, b_1, n, a_k, \ldots, a_1)$$
Since $b_m < \cdots < b_1 < n > a_k > \cdots > a_1$, this is unimodal. So **every** $g \in U_n$ satisfies $g \circ \text{rev} \in U_n$, giving $2^{n-1}$.

Therefore $M(n) = 2^{n-1}$.

## Computing $m(n)$: the pair-swap permutation

Define $\rho_0$ to swap adjacent pairs: $\rho_0 = (2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, \ldots)$ (for odd $n$, the last element stays fixed). I claim $g \circ \rho_0 \notin U_n$ for every $g \in U_n$ when $n \geq 4$.

**Proof of claim.** Write $g = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ with peak at position $p$ (so $a_p = n$). Then $g \circ \rho_0 = (a_2, a_1, a_4, a_3, \ldots)$.

The *within-pair* differences of $g \circ \rho_0$ at positions $2i-1$ are $a_{2i-1} - a_{2i}$, which are the **negations** of $g$'s differences at odd positions. Since $g$ is unimodal:
- Pairs fully in the increasing part of $g$ ($2i < p$): $a_{2i-1} < a_{2i}$, so within-pair diff is **negative**.
- Pairs fully in the decreasing part ($2i-1 \geq p$): $a_{2i-1} > a_{2i}$, so within-pair diff is **positive**.

This creates a **valley pattern** (negative then positive) in the within-pair differences — the opposite of the peak pattern (positive then negative) required for unimodality.

**Case $p = 1$** ($g$ decreasing): All within-pair diffs are positive; all between-pair diffs ($a_{2i+1} - a_{2i-1} < 0$) are negative. Signs alternate $+, -, +, -, \ldots$, giving multiple sign changes. Not unimodal. ✗

**Case $p = n$** ($g$ increasing): All within-pair diffs are negative; all between-pair diffs are positive. Signs alternate $-, +, -, +, \ldots$. Not unimodal. ✗

**Case $1 < p < n$**: Let $p$ fall in pair $j$. Pairs $1, \ldots, j{-}1$ (or $j$) have negative within-pair diffs; pairs after have positive within-pair diffs. So there exist positions $r < s$ with within-pair diff negative at $r$ and positive at $s$. For unimodality, all diffs before the peak must be positive and all after must be negative. But a negative diff at position $r$ forces the peak at position $\leq r$, while a positive diff at position $s > r$ forces the peak at position $> s$ — contradiction. ✗

For odd $n$, the unpaired last element adds one more difference but cannot resolve the valley pattern already present in the first $n-1$ elements (which contain at least 2 pairs when $n \geq 5$).

**Verification for $n = 4$**: With $\rho_0 = (2,1,4,3)$, I checked all 8 unimodal permutations — none compose to a unimodal permutation. For $n = 5$ with $\rho_0 = (2,1,4,3,5)$, exhaustive case analysis by peak position confirms 0.

Therefore $m(n) = 0$ for all $n \geq 4$.

## Final Computation

$$\sum_{n=4}^{10} \bigl(M(n) + m(n)\bigr) = \sum_{n=4}^{10} \bigl(2^{n-1} + 0\bigr) = \sum_{k=3}^{9} 2^k = 2^{10} - 2^3 = 1024 - 8 = \boxed{1016}$$
